blocks.text: Almost every backend application stores data in a relational database. Plain JDBC works, but you write the same code again and again: open a connection, prepare a statement, bind parameters, loop over a `ResultSet`, copy columns into objects, close everything. Object-relational mapping (ORM) removes that work. You describe how a class maps to a table, and a library generates the SQL. In the Spring world the stack has three layers, and interviewers like to hear you separate them.

rows: A specification: annotations such as `@Entity` and an API (`EntityManager`). It is only interfaces and rules, no code that talks to a database.
The most common JPA implementation (the "provider"). It generates SQL, tracks changes and caches objects. Spring Boot uses it by default.
A Spring layer on top of JPA. You declare an interface and Spring generates the repository implementation for you at startup.
blocks.caption: Three names that are often confused.

blocks.text:
The packages are `jakarta.persistence.*` in Spring Boot 3 and 4 (older tutorials show `javax.persistence`, which no longer works).

### Dependencies and configuration

Add the starter and a driver. H2 is an in-memory database that is perfect for learning and tests; PostgreSQL is what you would run for real.

blocks.code:
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
    <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
blocks.title: pom.xml (dependencies)

blocks.text: With H2 on the classpath and no datasource configured, Boot starts an embedded in-memory database automatically. For PostgreSQL you give the URL and credentials. Keep the password out of the file (see the chapter on configuration in Part 1) and read it from an environment variable.

blocks.code:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/library
spring.datasource.username=library
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
blocks.title: application.properties

blocks.text:
Boot builds a connection pool (HikariCP) for you. You normally do not set the dialect any more; Hibernate detects it from the connection.

### Entities

An entity is a class that maps to a table. It needs `@Entity`, an `@Id` field, and a no-argument constructor (JPA creates objects by reflection; the constructor may be `protected`). Entities cannot be records, because Hibernate needs to set fields after construction and may subclass the class to build proxies.

blocks.title: Book.java

blocks.text: What to notice. `@GeneratedValue(strategy = IDENTITY)` lets the database assign the id (auto-increment column), so `id` is `null` until the row is inserted. `@Column` is optional: without it the field maps to a column with the same name. Boot's default naming strategy turns `copies` into `copies` and `firstName` into `first_name`. Do not use a primitive `long` for the id, because a new object must be able to say "I have no id yet".

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` is the usual choice on PostgreSQL because it lets Hibernate batch inserts; `IDENTITY` forces an immediate insert to learn the id. For a beginner project `IDENTITY` is simpler and fine.

### The persistence context and entity states

Hibernate does not run SQL the moment you call a setter. It keeps loaded entities in a first-level cache called the **persistence context** (one per `EntityManager`, which in a Spring app usually means one per transaction). Every entity instance is in one of four states.

blocks.alt: save close | Transient Managed Detached | new Book() tracked by context context closed | remove | changes to managed entities | Removed | are written at flush or commit | delete at flush

blocks.text:
- **Transient (new):** created with `new`, not known to JPA, no row.
- **Managed (persistent):** attached to the persistence context. Hibernate watches its fields ("dirty checking") and writes any change to the database when the transaction flushes.
- **Detached:** was managed, but its persistence context closed (typically the transaction ended). Changes are no longer tracked.
- **Removed:** scheduled for deletion at flush.

The consequence that surprises beginners: inside a transaction you do not have to call `save` after changing a managed entity. The change is saved automatically at commit.

blocks.title: BookService.java

blocks.text:
### Repositories

A Spring Data repository is an interface. You extend `JpaRepository<Entity, IdType>` and get CRUD and paging methods with no implementation code.

blocks.title: BookRepository.java

blocks.text: At startup Spring creates a proxy class implementing this interface and registers it as a bean, so you inject `BookRepository` like any other dependency. The inherited methods you use most:

rows: INSERT if the entity is new, otherwise merge (UPDATE). Returns the managed instance: use the return value.
All rows, sorted, or one page.
Remove; `deleteById` on a missing id does nothing in current versions.
blocks.caption: Common JpaRepository methods.

blocks.text:
#### Derived query methods

Spring parses the method name: `findBy` + property + keyword. `findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase` becomes `where` `lower(title) like %?%`. Keywords include `And`, `Or`, `Between`, `LessThan`, `GreaterThan`, `In`, `IsNull`, `OrderBy`, `Top`/`First`. If you misspell a property, the application fails at startup with a clear message, which is a feature: you find the bug immediately. Once the name gets long (three conditions or more), switch to `@Query`.

#### @Query and JPQL

JPQL looks like SQL but speaks in entities and fields (`Book`, `b.title`), not tables and columns. Always bind values with named parameters (`:q`), never by concatenating strings, which would be an SQL injection hole. Add `nativeQuery =` `true` when you need real SQL.

#### Paging and sorting

Never return an unbounded list from an API. Pass a `Pageable` and get a `Page` with the content plus total counts.

blocks.title: PagingExample.java

blocks.text:
In a controller you can simply declare a `Pageable` parameter and Spring fills it from `?page=0&size=20&sort=title,asc`. Return `Slice` instead of `Page` if you do not need the total, which saves the count query.

### Creating the schema: ddl-auto, schema.sql and Flyway

Hibernate can create tables from your entities. The switch is `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto`:

rows: Do nothing. The default for a real database.
Check that tables and columns match the entities; fail at startup if not. Good for production.
Try to alter tables to match. Never adds safety; can not rename or drop columns.
Drop and recreate the schema on startup (and drop on shutdown for `create-drop`). Only for tests.
blocks.caption: ddl-auto values.

blocks.text: Boot defaults to `create-drop` for an embedded database (H2) and `none` for everything else, which is why a demo "just works" and a PostgreSQL project does not create tables. In production the schema must be controlled by **versioned** **migration scripts**, not by Hibernate guessing. The standard tool is Flyway (Liquibase is the alternative). Add `flyway-core` (and `flyway-database-postgresql` for PostgreSQL on recent Flyway versions) and put numbered scripts in `src/main/resources/db/migration`; Boot runs them at startup before Hibernate validates.

blocks.title: db/migration/V1__create_books.sql

blocks.text: `schema.sql` and `data.sql` in `src/main/resources` also work and are simple, but they have no history, no checksums and no ordering across environments. Use them for demos and tests, Flyway for anything deployed.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never run `ddl-auto=update` or `create` against a production database. `create` deletes all data on the next restart. `update` silently drifts the schema away from what your team reviewed, and it cannot do destructive changes like renaming a column, so you end up fixing it by hand at 2 a.m. Use Flyway migrations plus `validate`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA? JPA is the specification (annotations and the `EntityManager` API). Hibernate is an implementation of that specification that generates SQL and tracks entity changes. Spring Data JPA sits on top: it generates repository implementations from interfaces and derived method names, and calls JPA/Hibernate underneath. You can use Hibernate without Spring Data, but not Spring Data JPA without a JPA provider.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does an update work without calling save()? A loaded entity inside a transaction is managed. At flush time Hibernate compares it with the snapshot taken at load time (dirty checking) and issues an UPDATE for any difference. `save()` is only required for new entities or for detached ones that you want to merge back.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- JPA is the specification, Hibernate the provider, Spring Data JPA the repository layer on top.
- An entity needs `@Entity`, `@Id` and a no-arg constructor; use `jakarta.persistence` imports.
- Managed entities are dirty-checked: changes inside a transaction are written at commit without `save`.
- Derived query names are checked at startup; use `@Query` with named parameters for anything longer.
- Return `Page` or `Slice` with a `Pageable`, never unbounded lists.
- Production schemas come from Flyway migrations with `ddl-auto=validate`, not from Hibernate generation.

sections.title: Relationships, transactions and the N+1 problem

blocks.text:
Real data has relationships: an author writes many books, a member borrows many books, a book has many categories. JPA maps these with four annotations, and almost every serious JPA bug comes from using them without understanding two things: who owns the relationship, and when related data is loaded. This chapter covers both, then the transaction rules that make multi-step changes safe.

### Mapping relationships

Think in terms of the **foreign key**. In a relational schema, the table that holds the foreign key column is the one that really stores the relationship. JPA calls it the **owning side**. The other side is optional, read-only convenience, and is marked with `mappedBy`.

blocks.title: Author.java
Book.java (relationship part)

blocks.text: What to notice. `@ManyToOne` on `Book` is the owning side and creates the `author_id` column. `mappedBy = "author"` on `Author.books` says "the field `author` in `Book` owns this". If you set only `author.getBooks().add(book)` and forget `book.setAuthor(...)`, nothing is written, because the owner was never set. That is why we use the helper methods `addBook` and `removeBook`.

rows: Many books, one author. FK in the "many" table.
One author, many books. Usually the inverse side of a `@ManyToOne`.
One to one, FK on one side.
Students and courses. Needs a join table (`@JoinTable`).
blocks.caption: The four relationship annotations.

blocks.text:
For `@ManyToMany`, the owning side declares `@JoinTable(name = "loan_books", joinColumns = ...,` `inverseJoinColumns = ...)`. In practice, when the join needs its own data (a loan has a date and a due date), do not use `@ManyToMany`: create a real `Loan` entity with two `@ManyToOne` fields. That is exactly what the project in Part 5 does.

### Cascade and orphan removal

`cascade` passes an operation from parent to children. With `CascadeType.ALL` on `Author.books`, saving an author saves its new books, and deleting an author deletes its books. `orphanRemoval = true` also deletes a book removed from the list. Use cascading only for real parent-owns-child aggregates (order and its lines). Do not put `CascadeType.REMOVE` on a `@ManyToOne` or on `@ManyToMany`: deleting one book must never delete the shared author.

### Lazy and eager fetching

**Eager** means "load the related data together with me". **Lazy** means "put a placeholder (a proxy) there and load the data only when somebody touches it". Lazy is almost always right, because eager loading drags whole object graphs into memory whether you need them or not. Notice the default for `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` is EAGER, so set `fetch =` `FetchType.LAZY` explicitly, as we did.

The price of lazy loading is `LazyInitializationException`: the proxy can only load data while its persistence context is open (inside the transaction).

blocks.title: LazyBug.java

blocks.text: The fix is not "make everything eager". Load what you need inside the transaction: put `@Transactional` on the service method, or better, fetch exactly the data required with a query (below).

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Spring Boot enables `spring.jpa.open-in-view=true` by default. It keeps the persistence context open during the whole web request, so lazy loading appears to work even in your controller and even when the service has no transaction. It hides the bug above, leaks database access into the web layer, and holds a connection longer. Boot logs a warning at startup. Most teams set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false` and fetch what they need in the service layer.

### The N+1 select problem

This is the most asked JPA question in interviews. You load a list of N authors with one query, then read each author's books. Each access to a lazy collection fires its own query: 1 query for the list plus N for the collections.

blocks.title: NPlusOne.java

blocks.text: **Typical SQL log (spring.jpa.show-sql=true), 3 authors**

blocks.code:
select a1_0.id, a1_0.name from author a1_0
select b1_0.author_id, b1_0.id, b1_0.title from book b1_0 where b1_0.author_id=?
select b1_0.author_id, b1_0.id, b1_0.title from book b1_0 where b1_0.author_id=?
select b1_0.author_id, b1_0.id, b1_0.title from book b1_0 where b1_0.author_id=?

blocks.text:
With 3 authors it is invisible. With 10,000 it is 10,001 round trips to the database and a slow endpoint that "worked fine on my machine". You find it by turning on SQL logging in development (`logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG`) and counting statements. There are three standard fixes.

#### Fix 1: join fetch

Tell JPQL to load the collection in the same query.

blocks.title: AuthorRepository.java

blocks.text:
One SQL join, one round trip. Limits: you cannot page a collection `join fetch` in the database (Hibernate pages in memory and warns), and fetching two collections at once at the same time multiplies rows.

#### Fix 2: @EntityGraph

The same idea without writing JPQL. It works on derived methods too.

blocks.title: AuthorRepository.java (alternative)

blocks.text:
#### Fix 3: DTO projection

If you only need a few fields, do not load entities at all. Select straight into a record. It is the fastest option, because there is no persistence context overhead and no lazy loading to trip over.

blocks.title: AuthorSummary.java

blocks.text: A fourth, less common tool is `@BatchSize` (or the property `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50`), which loads lazy collections for 50 parents at once, turning N queries into N/50. It is a cheap safety net, not a design.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it? One query loads N parent rows, then lazy access to a relationship on each parent fires N more queries. Fix by fetching the relationship in the initial query: `join fetch` in JPQL, `@EntityGraph`, or select a DTO projection that contains exactly the columns needed. Detect it by logging SQL and counting statements, or with a test that asserts the query count. Switching to EAGER does not fix it (Hibernate still issues the extra selects for `findAll`) and loads data you do not need.

### equals and hashCode on entities

Entities live in sets and maps, and Hibernate compares them. Two rules keep you safe. Do not use Lombok `@Data` or an IDE-generated `equals` over all fields, since fields change and lazy collections would be loaded just to compute a hash. And do not base equality on a database-generated `id` naively, because it is `null` before the first save, so the hash code would change after persisting an entity already placed in a `HashSet`.

A pragmatic pattern: equality on a natural business key that never changes (the ISBN), or the id only when non-null with a constant hash code.

blocks.title: Book.java (equality by natural key)

blocks.text:
Use `instanceof` rather than `getClass()` comparison, because Hibernate may hand you a subclass proxy. Do not include relationship fields in `toString` either, or you create infinite loops (author prints books, each book prints its author).

### Transactions

A **transaction** groups several database operations so that they either all succeed or all roll back (atomicity). A bank transfer that debits one account and credits another is the classic example. In Spring you declare it with `@Transactional` on a service method.

blocks.title: LoanService.java

blocks.text:
Spring wraps `LoanService` in a proxy (see the chapter on bean lifecycle and proxies in Part 1). The proxy begins a transaction before `borrow`, calls your code, then commits if it returns normally or rolls back if it throws.

#### The rules you must know

- **Rollback only on unchecked exceptions by default.** A `RuntimeException` or `Error` rolls back. A checked exception (such as `IOException`) commits! Declare `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` if checked exceptions should roll back.
- **Placement:** put it on public methods of Spring beans, in the service layer, not on repositories or controllers. A `private` or `final` method cannot be intercepted by the proxy.
- **Propagation** says what to do if a transaction already exists. The default `REQUIRED` joins the existing one, or starts a new one if none. So a service method calling another `@Transactional` method shares a single transaction, and an exception in the inner one marks the whole transaction rollback-only. `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the current transaction and runs the inner call in an independent one (use it for audit logging that must survive a rollback). Other values (`SUPPORTS`, `MANDATORY`, `NEVER`, `NESTED`) are rare.
- `readOnly = true` is a hint: Hibernate skips dirty checking and the driver may optimise. Use it on query methods. It is not a security guarantee.
- **Isolation** controls what concurrent transactions see of each other: `READ_COMMITTED` (the default on PostgreSQL) prevents dirty reads, `REPEATABLE_READ` also keeps repeated reads stable, `SERIALIZABLE` behaves as if transactions ran one by one and is the slowest. Leave the default unless you can name the anomaly you are preventing.

#### Self-invocation: the proxy limit

Because the transaction logic lives in the proxy, a call from one method to another method of the same object never passes through the proxy.

blocks.title: SelfInvocation.java

blocks.text: Fixes: move `archive` into another bean and inject it, or put `@Transactional` on the outer method as well. Calling from a controller or another bean works because that call goes through the proxy.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Catching an exception inside a `@Transactional` method and swallowing it prevents the rollback: the proxy sees a normal return and commits. Either rethrow, or deliberately design the catch as part of your business logic. Likewise, never keep a transaction open across a slow HTTP call to another service; it holds a database connection while waiting.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Does @Transactional roll back on a checked exception? By default, no. Rollback happens for `RuntimeException` and `Error`; a checked exception commits the work done so far. Use `rollbackFor` to change that. A second favourite follow-up: "Why does @Transactional not work when I call the method from another method in the same class?" Because Spring applies it through a proxy, and a `this.` call skips the proxy.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The side with the foreign key owns the relationship; `mappedBy` marks the inverse side, and you must set both sides in code.
- Make associations LAZY (set it explicitly for `@ManyToOne`/`@OneToOne`) and fetch what you need with `join fetch`, `@EntityGraph` or a DTO projection.
- N+1 is one list query plus one query per row's lazy relation; find it by counting logged SQL.
- `LazyInitializationException` means you touched a proxy outside the transaction; consider disabling open-in-view.
- `@Transactional` rolls back on unchecked exceptions only, joins existing transactions by default (`REQUIRED`), and works through a proxy, so self-invocation is not covered.
- Base entity `equals`/`hashCode` on a stable business key, never on all fields or on relationship collections.

Tests are what let you change code without fear, and interviewers expect you to know the difference between a fast unit test and a slow integration test. Spring Boot gives you a rich set of test tools, but the most important idea is not a tool: test each thing at the cheapest level that can still catch the bug.

### The test pyramid

**The test pyramid**

blocks.code:
/\
     /  \      few    end-to-end: whole app + real DB (@SpringBootTest, Testcontainers)
    /----\
   /      \    some   slice tests: one layer + Spring (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest)
  /--------\
 /          \  many   unit tests: plain Java + JUnit + Mockito, no Spring at all
/____________\

blocks.text:
Unit tests run in milliseconds because no Spring context is started. Slice tests start only the beans of one layer (a few hundred milliseconds to a couple of seconds). Full `@SpringBootTest` tests start the whole application and cost seconds each, and Spring caches the context between tests with the same configuration to soften that.

The starter `spring-boot-starter-test` (added by start.spring.io as a `test` dependency) brings JUnit 5 (Jupiter), AssertJ, Mockito, Hamcrest, JSONassert, JsonPath and Spring's test support.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Spring Boot 4 splits test support into per-technology test starters, for example `spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test` for MVC tests and `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test` for JPA tests. Generate the project on start.spring.io and tick the starters you use, and it adds the matching test starters. Spring Boot 3.5 only needs `spring-boot-starter-test`. The test annotations are the same names; in Boot 4 some of them live in new packages, so let the IDE fix imports. This chapter marks the differences.

### Unit tests without Spring

Keep business logic in plain classes with constructor injection (as the previous Parts recommended), and you can test it with `new`. Mockito replaces the collaborators, AssertJ gives readable assertions.

blocks.title: LoanServiceTest.java

blocks.text: What to notice. There is no Spring annotation in sight: `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` is Mockito's JUnit 5 extension, `@Mock` creates the fakes and `@InjectMocks` calls the constructor with them. `when(...).thenReturn(...)` stubs a call; `verify(...)` checks an interaction happened (or, with `never()`, did not). Name tests after behaviour (`borrowFailsWhenNoCopiesLeft`), and follow arrange, act, assert.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Mockito by default (strict stubs under `MockitoExtension`) fails a test that stubs a call it never uses. That is useful: it flags dead setup. Do not mock what you do not own (such as `String` or a JDK collection) or simple value objects like `Book`; use real instances.

### Controller tests with @WebMvcTest

`@WebMvcTest(BookController.class)` starts only the web layer: the controller, JSON conversion, validation, `@RestControllerAdvice`, and security filters. It does not create services or repositories, so you provide fakes with `@MockitoBean`. `MockMvc` then sends requests to the `DispatcherServlet` without opening a network port.

blocks.title: BookControllerTest.java

blocks.text: What to notice. `@MockitoBean` (from Spring Framework 6.2) replaces the old `@MockBean`, which is removed in Boot 4; it registers a Mockito mock in the test's application context. The third test shows the value of this slice: validation and the error handler run, with no service and no database. In Boot 3.5 `@WebMvcTest` is in `org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet`; in Boot 4 it moved to `org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure` and needs `spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test`. `get`/`post`/`jsonPath` are unchanged.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: If your app has Spring Security, `@WebMvcTest` includes the security filter chain, so requests return 401 or 403 until you authenticate. Add `@WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")` on the test (needs `spring-security-test`), or `.with(csrf())` for POSTs when CSRF is enabled. Do not "fix" it by deleting security from the test; you would stop testing the real rules.

### Repository tests with @DataJpaTest

`@DataJpaTest` starts only JPA: entities, repositories, a `TestEntityManager`. It replaces your datasource with an embedded H2 database (if on the classpath) and wraps each test in a transaction that rolls back afterwards, so tests do not pollute each other.

blocks.title: BookRepositoryTest.java

blocks.text: Test your own queries (derived methods with more than one condition, `@Query` strings, paging), not the `save` and `findById` that Spring Data already tested. In Boot 3.5 the annotation is in `org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa`; in Boot 4 it moved to `org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure` (companion starter `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test`). Check the import your IDE offers.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: An in-memory H2 database is not PostgreSQL. SQL that works on H2 can fail in production (JSON columns, `ilike`, sequences, locking). For queries that matter, run the test against the real engine with Testcontainers (below), or at least H2 in `MODE=PostgreSQL`.

### Full-stack tests with @SpringBootTest

`@SpringBootTest` loads the complete application context. With `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` it also starts the real embedded server on a random free port, and you call it over HTTP.

blocks.title: LibraryApiIT.java
Note
blocks.text: In Boot 4, `@SpringBootTest` no longer provides `TestRestTemplate` or `MockMvc` automatically. Add `@AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate` (plus the `spring-boot-resttestclient` test dependency; the class lives in `org.springframework.boot.resttestclient`) or `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`. The newer `RestTestClient` (enabled with `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient`) is the recommended replacement for `TestRestTemplate` and has a fluent `expectStatus()` / `expectBody()` style like `WebTestClient`. In Boot 3.5 only the listing above is needed.

Full-stack tests are slow and blunt, so write few of them: one per main use case (create, read, borrow, return). They prove the pieces are wired together: component scanning, configuration, Flyway migrations, security, serialisation.

### Real databases with Testcontainers

Testcontainers starts a throwaway Docker container (here PostgreSQL) for your tests, so tests run against the same engine as production. Spring Boot integrates it with `@ServiceConnection`, which configures the datasource from the running container, with no URL to write.

blocks.title: PostgresIT.java (needs Docker and testcontainers dependencies)

blocks.text:
You need the `spring-boot-testcontainers`, `org.testcontainers:junit-jupiter` and `org.testcontainers:postgresql` test dependencies (Boot 4 packages differ slightly; the Testcontainers site documents the BOM versions) and a running Docker daemon. It is the best way to make Flyway migrations and native queries trustworthy. To keep the build fast, reuse one container across test classes with a shared static container to keep the build fast.

### Which annotation for which job

rows: Business logic in services, mappers, validators
Status codes, JSON shape, validation, error responses
A few end-to-end flows, wiring checks
Replace a bean (service, client) in a slice test
blocks.caption: Test annotations at a glance.

blocks.text:
### What to test

- **Business rules and branches**: the borrow limit, the "no copies left" path, boundary values (0, 1, max).
- **Contracts at the edge**: status codes, validation errors, error body, JSON field names. These are what clients depend on.
- **Your queries and mappings**: custom `@Query`, unique constraints, cascades.
- **Failure paths**: not found, duplicate, invalid input, unauthorised. Bugs live here.
- **Do not test**: getters and setters, Spring itself, or private methods. Test through the public behaviour.

Make tests independent (no test relies on another test's data), deterministic (inject a `Clock` instead of calling `LocalDate.now()`), and fast. Run them with `./mvnw test`; by convention Maven's Surefire plugin runs classes named `*Test` and Failsafe (`./mvnw verify`) runs `*IT`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between @Mock and @MockitoBean (formerly @MockBean)? `@Mock` is plain Mockito: it creates a fake object, no Spring involved, ideal for unit tests with `@InjectMocks`. `@MockitoBean` creates a Mockito mock and registers it in the Spring `ApplicationContext`, replacing any bean of that type, so Spring injects the fake into the controller or service under test. `@MockBean` did the same job and was deprecated in Boot 3.4 and removed in Boot 4.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why prefer @WebMvcTest over @SpringBootTest for a controller? It starts only the web layer, so it is much faster and tests exactly what the controller is responsible for: mapping, validation, serialisation and error handling. Collaborators are mocked, so failures point at the controller. Use `@SpringBootTest` sparingly to prove the layers are wired together.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Test at the cheapest level: many plain unit tests, some slice tests, few full `@SpringBootTest` runs.
- Unit tests need no Spring: constructor injection plus Mockito and AssertJ.
- `@WebMvcTest` + `MockMvc` + `@MockitoBean` tests the web layer; `@DataJpaTest` tests your queries with automatic rollback.
- `@MockitoBean` replaces `@MockBean`; in Boot 4 also check package changes and the added `@AutoConfigure...` annotations on `@SpringBootTest`.
- Use Testcontainers when the real database engine matters (migrations, native SQL).
- Test behaviour and failure paths, not getters or the framework.
#### Spring Data JPA basics

items.question: Which of JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA is only a specification?
items.answer: JPA (Jakarta Persistence). Hibernate implements it; Spring Data JPA builds on it.

items.question: A method in a `@Transactional` service does `book.setTitle("X");` on an entity it loaded with `findById` and returns. Is the title updated in the database? Why?
items.answer: Yes. The entity is managed, so dirty checking issues an UPDATE when the transaction commits; no `save` call is needed.

items.question: What happens at startup if you declare `List<Book> findByTitel(String t)` in the repository?
items.answer: The context fails to start: Spring cannot find a property named `titel` on `Book` and reports it.

items.question: What is wrong with `@Query("select b from Book b where b.title = '" + t + "'")`, and what is the fix?
items.answer: String concatenation allows SQL/JPQL injection (and it will not compile as an annotation value anyway if `t` is not a constant). Use a named parameter `:t` with `@Param("t")`.

items.question: Which `ddl-auto` value would you use with Flyway in production, and why?
items.answer: `validate` (or `none`): Flyway owns the schema, Hibernate only checks that it matches.

items.question: Can a Java `record` be an `@Entity`? Give one reason.
items.answer: No: JPA needs a no-arg constructor, mutable fields and the ability to subclass the class for lazy proxies; records are final and immutable. Use records for DTOs instead.

blocks.text: #### Relationships, transactions and the N+1 problem

items.question: In the `Author`/`Book` mapping above, which side owns the relationship and how do you know?
items.answer: `Book`, because it has the `@ManyToOne` with the `@JoinColumn`; the foreign key column lives in its table. `Author.books` is the inverse side (`mappedBy`).

items.question: You write `author.getBooks().add(book);` and save the author, but `book.author_id` is null. Why?
items.answer: The owning side `Book.author` was never set. Update both sides (helper method `addBook`).

items.question: What is wrong here, and what exception do you expect? `Book b = repo.findById(1L).get(); return` `b.getAuthor().getName();` in a method without `@Transactional`, with `open-in-view=false`.
items.answer: `LazyInitializationException`: the author proxy is touched after the persistence context closed. Fetch the author in the query or add a transaction.

items.question: A page lists 50 authors with their book counts and takes 51 SQL statements. Name the problem and two fixes.
items.answer: N+1 select. Fix with `join fetch` / `@EntityGraph`, or a DTO projection with `count` and `group by`.

items.question: A `@Transactional` method throws `new IOException("disk")`. Is the data rolled back?
items.answer: No. Checked exceptions do not trigger rollback by default; add `rollbackFor = Exception.class`.

items.question: Method `a()` of a bean calls `this.b()` which is annotated `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)`. How many transactions are created by calling `a()` from outside?
items.answer: Zero, unless `a()` itself is transactional: the `this.b()` call bypasses the proxy so the annotation on `b` is ignored.

blocks.text: #### Testing Spring Boot applications

items.question: Which test type would you write for "returns 409 when the ISBN already exists" in the controller, and which annotation supplies the service?
items.answer: A `@WebMvcTest` with MockMvc; `@MockitoBean BookService` throws the "duplicate" exception and the test expects status 409.

items.question: What does this print? Why? `@DataJpaTest` test A saves a `Book` and ends; test B calls `books.count()` first thing.
items.answer: B sees 0 rows (if the table was empty before): each `@DataJpaTest` test runs in a transaction that is rolled back at the end, so test A's data is gone.

items.question: A `@WebMvcTest` for a secured controller returns 401. Name two ways to fix the test without disabling security.
items.answer: Authenticate the request with `@WithMockUser(...)` or a `jwt()` / `httpBasic()` request post-processor; add `csrf()` for state-changing requests when CSRF is on.

items.question: Why can `@DataJpaTest` with H2 give you false confidence, and what is the remedy?
items.answer: H2 differs from PostgreSQL in SQL dialect, types and locking. Run the repository tests on the real engine with Testcontainers.

items.question: What is wrong: `@Autowired private BookService service;` inside a class annotated only `@WebMvcTest(BookController.class)`?
items.answer: `@WebMvcTest` does not create `@Service` beans, so the context fails with a missing bean. Use `@MockitoBean` for the service.

items.question: What does `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` do that the default mock environment does not?
items.answer: It starts a real embedded server on a random free port, so you test over actual HTTP using `TestRestTemplate` or a client, including servlet filters.
